utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Pasic, good morning to you as well. I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony still binds you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the last thing we were speaking about yesterday was the conversation you said you had with Mr. Basic, the one you had after you were called by the Tribunal and told when you would be a witness in this case. And you said that that conversation was on the 2nd of October. The 2nd of October was last Friday. Is that right, then? The conversation you had with Mr. Basic was last Friday?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the call you received from the Tribunal scheduling your testimony, did you receive that call the day before, earlier on that same day? When did you receive the telephone call from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the International Tribunal. It was Mrs. Lily, that was her name, on Friday, the 2nd of October, at around 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon. I was a little surprised when she told me that, on the 6th of October, I was supposed to be at The Hague Tribunal. I felt rather afraid and uncomfortable, because I'm 67 years old, and I've never been in a courtroom. And now suddenly I was forced to come -- well, I was supposed to come before a Tribunal of this stature. I called Mr. Basic to tell him the news, to say I had been called to appear and that I'd like to meet with him. Mr. Basic at that time happened to be travelling. He was going from Sibenik to Split. And I asked him to come to Sibenik, to have a cup of coffee, and to discuss the matter over a coffee.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, again, yesterday when I asked you about this initial conversation you had with Mr. Basic when you telephoned him, you said, and I'm going to quote from what you said yesterday: "I said that I had received information, telling me that I was going to be a witness, and I was told when and at what time. And then I saw that I was in a bit of a predicament since some statements that I had given to the Prosecutors in 2002 do not stand, since I changed a part with respect to General Cermak. I was supposed to change -- well, as far as I was concerned, as a commissioner of the Croatian government, these statements do not stand, as far as the events that happened after Operation Storm are concerned as well." Now, when you said "as a commissioner of the Croatian government, these statements do not stand," were there parts of your 2002 statement that you considered should not be a part of your evidence in this trial because of a position that you have held with the Croatian government, either back in 1995 or currently?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My answers have almost nothing to do with that, whether I occupied the post of commissioner of the government or this now. I looked carefully this morning, and I feel that the investigator had 77 questions, and I corrected only 12 of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you've said that your "... answers have almost nothing to do with that, whether I occupied the post of commissioner of the government." If that's the case, why did you say yesterday: "As a commissioner of the Croatian government, these statements do not stand."?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I received this duty to solemnly come before this Tribunal, then I said that the answers I gave to the investigators that I cannot take the solemn declaration saying I would tell the truth because there is no truth there which was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last phrase, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the interpreters didn't hear the last phrase you said. You said: "I cannot take the solemn declaration saying that I would tell the truth because there is no" --

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in part of the statement, which was given to the investigators, there is no truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you didn't answer my question, which was: Why did you say yesterday that "as a commissioner of the Croatian government, these statements do not stand." Why did you mention the fact that you were a commissioner of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I gave the statement, I was not a commissioner of the Croatian government. Therefore, a statement of that kind, whether I was or wasn't, would be like that whether I was or wasn't a commissioner of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the Chamber would like you or could I even take some steps ourselves, further explore what happened on that Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was -- that's -- if Your Honours would like to do that I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From a factual point of view --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- Going to do that. JUDGE ORIE -- before we go into the why's and et cetera, what exactly happened on that Friday. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, taking His Honour's directions, you -- you phoned Mr. Basic, you told him you wanted to meet with him in person, and he came to Sibenik to meet with you. And you met with him. Was that also on the Friday, that you met with Mr. Basic on -- in person?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Basic, both on Friday the 2nd, and on Saturday, the 3rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In both occasions, that was in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, on -- and, sorry, was that at your home in Sibenik where you met with him, in your house?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In a cafe. If you want me to tell you it's called Barun near Solaris.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on Friday when you met with Mr. Basic in the cafe, how long was that meeting? How many hours or minutes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the meeting lasted some 10, 15, 20 minutes when I asked Mr. Basic how and in what way was I to behave to adapt to the situation, how am I to behave when I come before this august Tribunal. We didn't discuss anything apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I take it, at that meeting, you decided to meet with him again the next day? You arranged to meet the next day with Mr. Basic as well; is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And why was that? Why did you arrange to meet him the next day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because I felt the need to talk to him once again. Mr. Basic is -- well, he was a little nervous as well. He might have felt that there was some -- there was some pressure or threats against me, but I categorically rejected that. I said there was no pressure, no threats, nor anything else prior to my leaving for The Hague Tribunal. As far as my departure here and coming in here, only my immediate family knows about that. My wife, who's in Italy over the phone, my son and his wife. And my son has actually come here with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the meeting you had with Mr. Basic on Saturday, how long was that meeting? How many hours or minutes did you meet with Mr. Basic on Saturday?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was about an hour; that's how long the meeting lasted. Mr. Basic suggested to me that, for the Tribunal, I should prepare in such a way as to check through both the statements I'd given. He -- we parted; we said good-bye; and -- to The Hague -- see you in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At either of these meetings on Friday or Saturday, did you discuss with Mr. Basic the changes that you wanted to make to your 2002 statement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not discuss that, but when I understood the levity [as interpreted] and seriousness of the statements given, I suddenly felt mistrustful towards myself. And from Zagreb to Amsterdam, I thought about all this, and I decided, I reached a decision, and decided to change part of the statement I'd given to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, earlier you said that when you initially telephoned Mr. Basic you told him that there was some statements you had given to the Prosecutors in 2002 that do not stand, "since I changed a part with respect to General Cermak, I was supposed to change" ... blah, blah, blah, et cetera, et cetera. When you initially phoned Mr. Basic, you told him you wanted to change parts of your statement. Are you saying that on the same day and on the next day that you met with Mr. Basic you never discussed any of the changes you wanted to make to your statement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not because part of the statements which I had given earlier referred to General Cermak and, later on, in reading through my own statements, I felt that there were quite a lot of bad statements regarding me and the relationship to -- of the Croatian government towards me as the former commissioner for Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, sorry, I'm a little confused because it seems to me that when you called - from what you're saying - when you called Mr. Basic initially your main concern was that there were statements that you had made that you wanted to change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There was statements that do not stand. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's not what the witness said in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- Could we -- Ms. Gustafson, of course, the witness said something about it yesterday. He said something about it today. Could you please refer to the exact portion of his evidence. If you give me page and line numbers then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's transcript page 22793.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. That's yesterday's transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. Beginning at line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 22793. I still have the old page numbering for the 8th of October, so I have --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It should be page 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 77, thank you. Page 77, you said line 21. Yes, now there is a difference in page numbering as well. Could you give me one word from that line, so with WordWheel I will be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's -- the line began: "I said that I had received information ..." Is the beginning of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "... received information ..." Yes, I have got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Court will recollect there is an lot of uncertainty over dates, 2nd of October, 10th of October, days of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it may be -- I would refer the Court to the beginning of his testimony on this -- this matter when he refers to being in a hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And making a telephone call there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm trying to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- perhaps we go through it briefly again, Ms. Gustafson. You phoned Mr. Basic once you had received information that you expected to go to The Hague, by Ms. Lily. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Where were you when you phoned him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in my flat in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you had a phone number of Mr. Basic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that a mobile phone number or is it ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A mobile phone number, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I will take it step by step. Do you know where Mr. Basic was when he answered your call on his mobile phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I called him up over the mobile phone, he was on his way from Sibenik to Split -- and Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At what time did you call him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was about 5.00, 5.30, I can't remember the exact time, but I think that's when it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that was almost immediately after you had received the phone call from Ms. Lily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you said you wanted to meet with him. At what time did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was -- well, in view of the fact that it's quite close to Sibenik, I think we met at about 6.00 or half past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- what now was exactly the reason why you called him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said before that I felt a certain dose of nervousness and some kind of pressure, so I asked him -- well, he could not come -- decided not to come, but I asked him to come and meet with me, to help me, and tell -- help me with how I was to behave before such an august auditorium as this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Now, we know, you told us yesterday, that you had met with the Defence approximately a month earlier, early September as well. Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How, in early September, was the arrangement made to meet with the Defence? Did you call them? Did they call you? So I'm now not talking about a week ago, but I'm talking about five weeks ago. Do you remember? Who then took the initiate for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were at a meeting one afternoon in Primosten at the proposal of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was -- was Mr. Basic present during that meeting as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Had you -- had he phoned you to come to that meeting, or had you phoned him to come to that meeting, or was the meeting in any other way arranged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence called me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, yesterday, the following - and let's, at this moment, for a moment not focus on the date. You were asked: "So you phoned him?" And then a date was mentioned. And you said what. And then your answer was the following. You said: "I said that I had received information telling me that I was going to be a witness." Now my first question is: When you said this yesterday, were you referring to what information exactly? Was that the phone call you received from Ms. Lily or any other information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was information that followed Ms. Lily's call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that was the phone call you made to Mr. Basic immediately after you had received Ms. Lily's phone call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, just forgive me for a second, but I'm now -- I'm deprived from my earlier transcript, and I have to get a new one. I apologise, but I'm just -- the old transcript has been removed and I have to find -- you said it was 22 thousand, 7 hundred and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: 793, Your Honour, line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you yesterday answered a question about that phone call, that was the phone call you made to Mr. Basic once you had received the information from Ms. Lily. And I now read the other portions of your answer. So the answer started with: "I said that I had received information, telling me that I was going to be a witness," which we now understand is the information you received from Ms. Lily, "and I was told when and at what time." And then you said: "And then I saw that I was in a bit of a predicament since some statements that I had given to the Prosecutors in 2002 do not stand, since I changed a part with respect to General Cermak." Now you say: "Then I saw that I was in a bit of a predicament since the statements do not stand." And you said: "I was supposed to change -- well, as far as I was concerned, as a commissioner of the Croatian government, these statements do not stand." Now you told us this when you answered a question about what you said during the telephone call with Mr. Basic. So what I'd like to know is whether this - that is, awareness that the previous statement does not stand - whether that was on your mind when making that phone call.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During my telephone conversation with Mr. Basic, I didn't refer to the statements that I had given and to the possible corrections of them at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question was whether that was on your mind at that moment; that there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you met with Mr. Basic. And can you tell us in a bit more -- you said he was nervous. How did you know that he was nervous? What made you feel that he was nervous? Did he say anything or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that Mr. Basic was nervous. I was nervous and uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's, then, go back to one of your previous answers. You said, at least when talking about the meeting for the next day, you said: "Mr. Basic is -- well, it [sic] was a little nervous as well. He might have felt that there was some -- there was some pressure or threats against me, but I categorically rejected that." So I understood this answer to be that Mr. Basic was nervous about the thought, that there might have been pressure upon you. What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't say anything, apart from asking me what I was feeling like. And I told him that I wasn't feeling that well. He asked me if I had any problems. I said no. He said did I experience any sort of pressure or threats. And I said no, none of that. Because, as I told him, no one outside of my close family knew that I was going to testify in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, may I take it you didn't tell anyone else; is that what you want to say? Because what other people know is often difficult to -- to fully know about yourself. You didn't tell anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, back to the first meeting, you said -- could you say a bit more in detail what did you then tell to Mr. Basic. How did you start your conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which meeting are you referring to? The one in Primosten or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the meeting one week ago, on Friday, once you had called Mr. Basic on his mobile phone. He then came to Sibenik, from what I understand, and then you had a meeting of short duration, 15 minutes. What did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me, when I asked him how to prepare myself, that there was nothing special that I should do, other than, Mr. Pasic, your task is to closely examine and review the statements you gave to The Hague investigators, the OTP investigators, and the Defence for General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, from what I understand, one month earlier, in Primosten, you had had a meeting in which you had, I take it, gone through your statements. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I asked to meet with him, because once I received an official call to appear before the ICTY, I felt that this was a very special occasion, and it affected me in a special way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that -- now, he told you, Just review your statement and that's all you have to do. Then what caused you to arrange for a meeting on the day after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was on his own, and I was on my own, and we simply met up to have another chat over coffee, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, that's -- when were you expected to travel, on what day? You met with Mr. Basic on Friday. You met again with him on Saturday. When did --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. That's correct. I left for Zagreb on Monday at 4.00, roughly. I spent the night in Zagreb in a hotel, and on the following morning, at 8.00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. I asked you when you left. That was on Monday, from what I understand. Now, you had a meeting of 15 minutes. And you were on -- he was on his own, you were on his [sic] own, and you said -- and we simply met up to have another chat over coffee. About what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the earlier statement, I said that Mr. Zeljko, when we were having that coffee, asked me, probably when he saw a certain degree of nervousness on my part, he asked me -- he saw that I was uneasy and anxious, so he asked me if there was any sort of pressure that had been excerpted upon me or any threats I might received, and I said that there were no problems as regards myself and my departure there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was on Friday, when you first met with him on that Friday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But I'm trying to find out what caused you, when you had met on Friday, what caused you to have another meeting on Saturday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't consider it a meeting. As a host, I wanted -- as a good host, I wanted to see Zeljko off and bid him a safe journey. So we had a cup of coffee and that was all. There were no notes taken, nothing of that sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that was all already known on Friday, isn't it, that you said you -- "I wanted to see Zeljko off and bid him a safe journey." Why didn't do you that on Friday? Why to meet again the next day for a much longer time than on the first occasion, apparently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because he spent the night in Sibenik, from Friday to Saturday, and being a person, a local person, I wanted to be there for him in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say, He is not a resident of Sibenik, and when someone comes and sees me in Sibenik, I have some responsibility to make him feel comfortable. Is that why you had coffee on Saturday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see it as a responsibility; I see it simply as a human gesture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, some people consider human gestures to be a responsibility. But let's leave that apart. Mr. Pasic, you had discussed -- or at least you had discussed any possible pressure or threats. You had said there was no one. Now, apart from whether you had discussed it, on that Saturday morning, between Friday and Saturday, had you read again your statement? Because Mr. Basic had told you that one of the things you were supposed to do is to review your statement before you would testify, as a preparation. Did you, on that Friday or Saturday morning, look at these statements at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read them carefully on Saturday, not once but several times. I focussed on every single statement I had given and discerned errors that were either my own fault or the fault of the investigator questioning me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you reviewed these statements on Saturday. Now, was that before you met with Mr. Basic or after you met with Mr. Basic, on Saturday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following my meeting with Mr. Basic, although I had analysed them also after having met with Mr. Basic, upon my return home on Friday evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Friday evening you analysed the statements, then had you a meeting with Mr. Basic on Saturday, and then you read them again several times? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, after meeting Mr. Basic on Saturday morning, I had plenty of time to read through them repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said Friday evening you analysed them. You read them again on Saturday. Did you already discern any possible matter which would need to be corrected on that Friday evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I discerned plenty of issues, and I told you that I corrected only 13 out of 77 paragraphs. So that was the bare minimum of what could have and should have been corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you receive a message that you have to go to the Tribunal to testify from Ms. Lily. You phone Mr. Basic. You know Mr. Basic to be a member of the Defence team. Please correct me when I'm wrong. Then Mr. Basic tells you that it is important to review your statements. Then you do that on Friday evening, if I understood you well. And you discern quite a number of errors, inaccuracies. Up until now, have I summarized your testimony accurately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not quite. The omissions that were down to me had been observed by me even before -- before the meeting in Primosten and before I had met Mr. Steven, the lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you told us that despite the fact that you may have at an earlier moment have already discerned a lot of inaccuracies or matters to be corrected, you read them again on Friday evening, after you had met with Mr. Basic, knowing that you would leave for The Hague the Monday after that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is necessary for me to go back to that and repeat this. As soon as I received a call to appear before the ICTY as a witness, the circumstances became very special, in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not challenging that at this moment. But then you met with Mr. Basic. Then you read again your statements on Friday evening and found that there was still a lot of inaccuracies. Then you met the next mourning with Mr. Basic, and after you had met with him, you, as you said, read your statements again. You read them over several times. Is that finding, again, that they were not, in every respect, true and correct? Is that a fair summary of what you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The moment I realised that my statements would be used before this Tribunal, my opinion changed completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your opinion about what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My opinion of the statements that had been given and that did not contain elements of what I had said and did contain certain statements that I had given without much thought, because I did not believe that they would be used anywhere and at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now earlier you told us that you had found out about inaccuracies already at an earlier stage, that you already, at an earlier moment - and let me -- you said: "The omissions that were down to me had been observed by me even before -- before the meeting in Primosten and before I had met Mr. Steven, the lawyer." So if you say, "my opinion changed," I do understand that you had already found the statement to be incorrect before you met one month ago in Primosten. So what now exactly changed, in your opinion, on that Friday or Saturday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing changed, either on Friday or on Saturday. Had Mr. Gotovina's lawyers been to see me, I would probably have had the time to review the statement I had given and change it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that you are referring to Mr. Cermak's lawyers or ... you said Mr. Gotovina's lawyers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. What I said was, Had I ever met them and talked to them, in that case, just as I had changed portions of my statements when I knew that I was going to appear for Mr. Cermak, I'm sure that the same would have happened had I discussed my statements with them, with the Gotovina team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why would you have changed the statement, if you have -- would have met with the Gotovina team lawyers? Why would that change your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't meet with me. But probably, had we analysed certain matters, as we did analyse them with Mr. Cermak, we would have arrived at different conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But your statement is about facts, or is it about conclusions you have drawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is about the facts that prevailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you had earlier met with members of the Cermak Defence team, and you said that you had already found, before the Primosten meeting, the statement to be inaccurate. I'm wondering what makes you change your statement, because that was before you met them. Did you tell them everything - that was one month ago - did you tell them all the points on which you considered your earlier statement to be inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Inaccurate interpretations of certain questions, certain issues, led me to change my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you tell -- you told me a couple of minutes ago that you had already found inaccuracies before the Primosten meeting. Had you read over your statements prior to the Primosten meeting, or did you read them at the Primosten meeting? Could you tell us? So I'm now talking about approximately a month ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read them in part; part of them in Primosten, and we analysed another part of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did you read them together with the members of the Defence team, or did you read them prior to the meeting in Primosten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read them prior to the meeting in Primosten, and we analysed them with the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you went through the statements paragraph by paragraph, or page by page, or just a free discussion on the whole of the statement? How did it take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it took place in the following manner: In part, I looked at the mistakes that I noticed and indicated the possibility of having those statements corrected. We did not analyse some other portions which did not have to do with the Cermak Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you focussed exclusively on what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I focussed on, exactly, on the Defence -- well, as a witness called by the Cermak Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you didn't see it fit, at that time, to correct also other parts of the statement, not directly in relation to Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I take you back to last week. First meeting with Mr. Basic on Friday, short meeting. Next day, Saturday morning, you had read already on Friday evening the statements again. Did you not at any point in time say to him, Well, I read the statement, and it's still not in every respect accurate. I'll come back to that. Or didn't you even mention what you found the evening before? That is, that the statement was still not accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the meeting on Saturday over a cup of coffee with Mr. Zeljko, neither of us uttered a single word about the statements, either of the Defence or the statements of the investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you, for the first time, then, raise this issue with the Defence? You had read them on Friday. You had read them several times on Saturday again. Did you give them a call? Did you in any way initiate any contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After I arrived in The Hague, I immediately called up Mr. Zeljko, and we met in the hotel assigned by the Registry. Mr. Basic came straightaway, and I told him that I felt the need to change part of the statement I had given to the investigators. He was a little surprised, but I insisted. And then he informed Mr. Steven, who also came. We had a meeting. And I was resolute and went point by point, looking to see which points I would change. And without any influence from them, I myself - thank God with their assistance - the contents that would be changed with the text that was in the previous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you had said you read the statements over on Friday; you read them again several times on Saturday. Did you have all the statements available to you on that Friday evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I'm talking about all the statements, I'm talking about the statements given to the investigators of the Prosecutor's office; I'm talking about the statement you later gave to the Defence; and the additional information you had given them in Primosten. Did you have all these three sources available to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have them all in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That - could I say - old statement given to the Prosecution, when did you receive a copy of that statement? I mean, since when did you have a copy of that statement in your possession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A copy of the statement given to the Prosecution I had in my possession since the time I first met with the lawyer, Mr. Cermak's lawyer, and that was -- I can't quite remember the date, but I do know that we were in Split for two days. I was on my way back to Knin. And we spent two days having talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that a little bit over half a year ago, or was that two years ago; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was last year. February or March, I can't be quite sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We find on one of your statements that an interview was held at the 17th and the 18th of February of this year. Would it be at that occasion? You said two days, and you said February or March --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. But then I said the wrong year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said last year, and ... it was two days. Now, being in possession of that statement, did you ever share the content of that statement with anyone? Did you ever discuss it with -- or, did you ever give it to read to any other person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you mean, anyone, any other person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any person in the world. Could be -- could be your children, your neighbours, your -- the local police, your former employer. Whoever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You kept it, and you never gave it to anyone to read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one -- well, I kept it for quite some time before I read it, and none of my family members even knew about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, if you with like to proceed, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, from the evidence that you have just given, I understand that it was on Friday evening and Saturday that you realised that your Prosecution statement had a number of errors. I think you mentioned 13, something like that. Is that -- is that right? It was Friday evening and Saturday that you realised that there were these mistakes in your statement that you needed to change?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood me. In reading part of those statements, I felt -- well, I felt this before, not only on Friday and Saturday. I felt that there was some mistakes before. Some of those errors related to me and to Mr. Cermak, and they were put right when I met the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the -- sorry, Mr. Pasic, if I could just ask you to put your papers away for now, and if you want to refer to them at some point, you can ask the Court. If you could just close your folder. Thanks. Now, according to the supplemental information sheet that was produced from the meeting that you had just on Tuesday with the Cermak Defence, it says: "On 6 October 2009, at 1600 hours, at a meeting to confirm his statement for the Rule 92 ter procedure, Mr. Pasic made the following corrections to his OTP statement, which was signed on 3 March 2002. "On his trip to The Hague on the plane, he carefully read his OTP statement after a long time, and he noticed, in certain paragraphs, sentences that do not correspond to what he said to the investigators during his interview. He acknowledges now that he did not properly review the OTP statement." Now, I take it from what you've just said that -- that that's not right, that -- where it says "he carefully read his OTP statement after a long time," you had in fact carefully read your OTP statement quite recently - on Friday and Saturday - and you had already noticed, before you were on the plane to The Hague, that there were sentences that did not correspond to what you said to the investigators. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Should we just make it clear: not right that he said it, or not right in terms of the information?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Otherwise things may be confused, and I'm concerned about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I take that you understand why Mr. Kay intervenes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Pasic, what I just read to you from that supplemental information sheet, that's not true, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand what -- you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, where it says in that supplemental information sheet: "On his trip to The Hague on the plane, he carefully read his OTP statement after a long time, and he noticed in certain paragraphs sentences that do not correspond to what he said to the investigators during his interview." That's not correct, that's not true. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is, that -- before -- that I had read the statements begin even before. And on my way to The Hague, I decided to change or to supplement the statements I had given.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, from your evidence yesterday, it's clear that you read this supplemental information sheet and you signed it, and then you told the Chamber that it was true. Why did you do that if, in fact, the sentence I just read to you isn't true?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson. Your statement that was put on paper this week, Tuesday, after you had arrived in The Hague says: "In the plane, when I went to The Hague, I read again my statements after a long time." Now, Ms. Gustafson, having heard your testimony, asks you whether that's true, because you just told us that you had read this statement on Friday and several times, again, on Saturday. So reading it on the plane was not after you had not seen them for a long time, because you had seen them a couple of days before. That's what Ms. Gustafson puts to you and says, What we find in this additional statement, therefore, is not true, because it was not after you had not seen those statements for a long time, but it was after you had read them over a couple of days before. And that she's seeking your comment on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I looked through them carefully on Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and Monday. And the decision about changing my statement -- well, I decided to do that after frequently having analysed them, and this decision was made when I was on the plane from Zagreb to Amsterdam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although you read the statements several times in the days before you were on the plane. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the reason why Ms. Gustafson asks you is because your statement says that you read them on the plane after you had not read them for a long time; whereas, you now tell us that you had read them during all these days several times. And so, therefore, not for the first time when you were on the plane.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that I started preparing myself in depth for coming in here at the time I was informed by Ms. Lily that I would be a witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear to us. Ms. Gustafson is seeking an explanation for what you tell us now, and you now repeat what you said before, and what we find in this second additional statement, that you read the statements on the plane after a long time; whereas, now you tell us that you had read them over again and again in the days before you went on the plane. So you had seen them briefly before being on the plane and not only after a long time, reading them again on the plane. We know what your testimony is, but Ms. Gustafson is seeking to understand why there is a difference between what we find in your Tuesday statement and what you just told us. Do you have any further explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have an explanation. But I see no reason for me, who have -- I have come in here to the Tribunal. I see no reason for me to read the statements a day or two before I come in here. I think I have enough sense to know that I have to prepare myself, and I said this at my meeting with Mr. Zeljko on Saturday, when he said, You must prepare and get to know the subject matter in both the two statements given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I think that the matter has been explored to an extent ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, we know that you - from your evidence today - we know you met with Mr. Basic on Saturday, and we know that you called him again when you arrived in The Hague on Tuesday. Between your meeting on Saturday with Mr. Basic, and when you telephoned him on Tuesday when you arrived in The Hague, did you have any communication with Mr. Basic or anyone else on the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for communication, from Saturday, when Mr. Basic left, to Tuesday, between myself and Mr. Basic or anybody else, no, there was no communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you were originally supposed to testify earlier this week, and then on Monday afternoon the Cermak Defence notified us that they were going to bring another witness in your place and move your testimony to later in the week. And I'm just wondering if, based on your information, your understanding of the events, if it's possible that the Cermak Defence already knew on Monday that you wanted to change your statement. Is that possible, based on your understanding of -- of events?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not certain --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May I just raise one matter here as I think it may be something not known by my learned friend. Mr. Dodig had a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Should we discuss this in the presence of the witness? I do not what you're going say, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a fact known by the Witnesses and Victims Unit that Mr. Dodig had a symposium on Thursday evening for 200 people that he had to address, and so we had to move him to give evidence earlier. So he had to shuffle up the pack, and Mr. Teskeredzic, as you know, is in hospital, or had been in hospital the previous week and was recovering from an operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson is now informed about this, and she'll certainly then consider this in her line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I ought to raise it to the Court's attention because Mr. Dodig's arrangements to be gone through the Registry, and he had to leave straightaway when he finished on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we have an issue that we may need to clarify in terms of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are close to the moment where we have a break. If it would be appropriate to deal with it in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if we can ask him to take his headphones off for just a sec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have not verified whether he speaks any English or not. Mr. Pasic, do you speak English? Do you speak any English, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well -- Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's just, I think, a little bit of uncertainty in the witness's answer at page 30, line 19. He was asked: "Is that possible, based on your understanding of events?" In Croatian he phrased it in such a way that in English it could be translated correctly by the interpreters as "It is not certain." Or, as I understood it, which was "Certainly not." And so those -- obviously that makes a difference in terms of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was a bit concerned about the way in which you phrased the question even in English, Ms. Gustafson. So perhaps we -- now you have additional information from Mr. Kay. You can consider then over the break whether or not it is of any use to rephrase it or to leave the matter as it is. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Somebody helping me has passed me a note: "Definitely not" was their review of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to Ms. Gustafson, being fed with a lot of information at this moment, how to pursue or how not to pursue this matter. Mr. Pasic, it's time for coffee.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I'm concerned, it's time for something else, not for coffee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Pasic, I'm not totally unfamiliar with the -- with the usual scheme of consumptions in the former Yugoslavia, but coffee is ready for you. We will have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to put on the record that the request for a videolink for Thursday, the 15th of October, has been, withdrawn, from what I understand, and I take it that at a later stage that we'll receive another request for the scheduling of such a videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber is inclined to move next week's Wednesday and Thursday's sessions to the morning. They are scheduled, at this moment, for the afternoon. And for a couple of reasons, the Chamber would prefer to sit in the morning on the Wednesday and Thursday, and would like to know whether there's any objection as far as the parties are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not for our part, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not for our part either, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Nor from our part, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then next week Wednesday, 14 October, and Thursday, 15th October, move to the morning. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could have D1706 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the statement, the 2002 statement that you gave to the Prosecution, is about to come up on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could have page 5 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'd like to direct your attention to the large paragraph in the middle of your screen, the one that begins: "Others at the meetings with Cermak ..." And I'd like you to just read that paragraph to yourself and then I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, is there anything in that paragraph that you did not say at the time you gave that statement that is, in fact, incorrect?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Save -- save for an addition that I'd like to make, which is the following: At these meetings, Mr. Cermak did not give any tasks either to me or to those present at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, you've now testified that you have read your statement probably six, seven, eight, nine times carefully, and you have never made any correction to that sentence. And you've told the Court that you read your statement several times, very carefully, because you realised the gravity of the situation of coming to testify. And you told the Trial Chamber that this statement, with the corrections that you made, that did not include any correction to this sentence, was true. Can you explain why you're changing it now?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because nobody has asked me about this so far. Regardless of my detailed review of my statements, I cannot recall all the details; I am 67 years old. I am aware of the fact that I'm prone to forgetfulness, and I am not a fit man, contrary to what you may think.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pasic, it may be that nobody asked you about this sentence so far, but, in fact, on the 2nd of September, when you met with the Defence, you corrected the statement -- the sentence immediately before this sentence. You said that the sentence, "After the liberation of Knin, the Sibenik logistics base came under Cermak in Knin," was not correct, and you didn't say that. Now, your testimony is that that sentence, about the Sibenik logistics base, is correct and you did say that, but it's not correct what's said in the following sentence. Now, which is it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please explain it to me once again? What is it that is controversial in the former or in the latter? The logistics base has nothing to do with the meetings and the rest, except for the fact that certain members of the logistics base were present at meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the issue is not what's controversial. The issue is what you said in your statement, and what you said on the 2nd of September, and what you're saying now. And I'm telling that you on the 2nd of September, you told the Cermak Defence that the sentence: "After the liberation of Knin, the Sibenik logistics base came under Cermak in Knin." You told them that that wasn't correct, and you didn't say that in your interview. Now you're saying, that that sentence is correct, you did say it in your interview, but it's not correct what's said in the sentence immediately following that. And I'm asking you: Which is it? Is it true what you said on the 2nd of September, or is it true what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered the question, Your Honour, in relation to the first matter, when put to him, and he raised it himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I disagree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, under the present circumstances, is allowed to put the question even if there would be some repetition in it. Ms. Gustafson, could you please repeat the question. Could you also try to keep your questions relatively short. We noticed that confusion easily is created, and it's for you to take care that it is avoided. Perhaps you rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the leave of the Bench, I think I'll just move on to the next point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we can move -- sorry, if we can stay on page 5 of the English and move to page 9 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the paragraph I'm interested now is the one in the middle of the screen that begins: "General Gotovina ..." Now, your 2002 statement says that General Gotovina was untouchable and unreachable, and that at social events he was surrounded by a lot of people; and at the end of these events, they would always sing Ustasha songs. And you've made a correction to that paragraph, that, essentially reverses what's stated here and your evidence -- your correct is that General Gotovina was approachable and that they only sang patriotic song, not Ustasha songs. Now, the word "Ustasha" is a very strong and very pejorative, negative word, isn't it? I think yesterday you referred to the fact that you were called a Ustasha commissioner, as ugly. Would you agree that that's an ugly word?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, generally speaking, you don't use that word lightly when you're referring to other people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never use that word.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, then, can you explain how it is that, if you never use that word, that when this statement was read to you in 2002, and when you read it again in November of 2007, and you read it again in February 2009, you either didn't notice this word or didn't bother to correct it on any of these occasions. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. I have told you now that there are countless statements there that I could change, but I noticed them at a time when I didn't know who to address these corrections to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, when you gave your statement to the Defence in 2007 and 2009, February, you did actually make a number of quite detailed corrections to your Prosecution statement. For example, at paragraph 12 of your Defence statement, you said: "In paragraph 18 of my statement to the Prosecution of 3 March 2002, it is necessary to amend the last sentence where I talk about having seen a soldier on a tractor with a ribbon around his head. This did not happen when I came to Knin on 6th August 1995 but two or three days later." So how is it that you found it important enough to change, correct the exact date on which you saw a soldier with a ribbon around his head when you gave your statement to the Defence, but you didn't correct what you say now is a false allegation of people singing Ustasha songs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I did correct both these allegations. On the issue of General Gotovina, I did correct my statement that one could reach him, that there were songs sung at social events, and if you sing songs like "Vila Velebita," "Ustani Bane," or "Jure and Boban," some may regard these songs as patriotic, whereas still others may perceive them differently. And I'm convinced that on that day, since the president was expected to arrive, this soldier with the bandana was not there. The -- the security situation was such that traffic was not allowed to pass, and, therefore, this person could not have been riding on -- on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, are you saying that songs like "Vila Velebita," "Ustani Bane," or "Jure and Boban," those types of songs were sung at the social events that you were talking about, that General Gotovina attended?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other -- others. Let me just state that just as is stated in the supplemental sheet, General Gotovina did not sing these songs, and during his short stay there, he exchanged a couple of words with the people present there and then proceeded to attend to his tasks. And those who did sing, they had to vent out their joy. Now, as for this soldier that I mentioned riding on the tractor, that was -- must have been his triumph there. That was his sentiment at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I just want to get back to the songs because you said about these songs: "Some may" -- record -- "some may perceive the songs as patriotic, whereas still others may perceive them differently."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, could I ask that the witness be invited to take his earphones off, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take your earphones off for a moment. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if we could first establish some foundation for these questions. We're assuming what kinds of songs are being sung, and we don't what we're talking about where, when, who is present. One of the issues that I was going to go into on cross before the change was sent the night before is that, as far as I know, there was one concert where General Forand was also present and the witness was present. I have a video-tape of the entire concert of over two hours, and we can go through songs and what songs are being sung there. If he's talking about events other than that concert, then I think some foundation should be established as to where and when and what we're talking about in fairness to the Defence so we can re-cross if necessary on this point. But there is no foundation at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, social events is already a plural. So apparently Ms. Gustafson is talking about something, not only a concert, perhaps even excludes the concert. But I take it, Ms. Gustafson, that you would be glad to put the answers of the witness in context. That is, what kind of events we're talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just add, I don't know of what foundation there is that this witness -- how many times he ever actually met or saw General Gotovina. I see, from what I can tell, one occasion that he has referenced in supplemental information sheets. So we don't even know, generally speaking, at this point, what the witness would say if asked how many times have you ever seen General Gotovina in your life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I mean, first of all, I'm primarily interested, at this point, in exploring the changes to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, secondly, this statement is the evidence of the -- with the corrections, is the evidence of the witness, tendered by the Defence. I don't think it's my obligation to explore a foundation for that. And, like I said, my primary focus with these questions is -- is the changes and the manner that they've been changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The difference in qualification of what the songs are patriot or Ustasha songs. That is what are you primarily -- and may I take it that this is done also in view of credibility and reliability testing, rather than to know exactly what songs were sung, where, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If in fact, Mr. President, I -- then I -- I'm happy with it if we're in agreement then that this is going to credibility and not for the truth of the matter asserted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said -- I used the word "primarily." So, therefore, to say if there is an agreement on that, then -- I understood this to be at this moment the primary focus of Ms. Gustafson' questions, I did not exclude in any way to establish what songs were sung. Let's -- Ms. Gustafson is now aware of the concerns you have. I would leave it in the hands of Ms. Gustafson, whether she would consider this in her further line of questioning or whether she would have to revisit the matter after you have again examined the witness, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. But again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- let me just state that it might be good to establish -- and actually fair to the Defence what the witness would say as to when he's ever had a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I said that Ms. Gustafson would certainly consider what you said, and you're now repeating what you said before, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I leave it in your hands. And you know what to expect if you deal not with those matters because then they will come back, and whether they come back pleasantly or as a boomerang is still to be seen. Could you put on your earphones again. Yes, Mr. Pasic, we will continue. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, Mr. Pasic. These songs that were talking about, you said: "Some ..." And I think there is it a mistake in the transcript. "Some may perceive these songs as patriotic, whereas still others may perceive them differently." Now, as far as you are aware, do some people perceive the songs that you mentioned as Ustasha songs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't received interpretation. I can hear them now. It wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's fixed again, Mr. Pasic, so listen carefully to the question Ms. Gustafson will put to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the question was: The songs that you mentioned you said: "Some may perceive the songs as patriotic, whereas still others perceive them differently." When you said "others may perceive them differently," would some people perceive those songs to be Ustasha songs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hardly. I listened to them, and I didn't feel that there was anything Ustasha-like in them. Perhaps "Jure and Boban," that particular song could be controversial in some segments, but not that much.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So would some people call that song a Ustasha song, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps they would. But not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how many occasions can you remember where you attended social events that General Gotovina also attended, after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I think that we were together at these parties where there was a guest appearance by the singer Krunoslav Cigoj then Krunoslav Kico Slabinac, another singer, as well as singers Hrid Matic, so perhaps we were there some three to four times.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And as far as you can recall, how many of those three to four times occurred in August or September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's been a long time since then. I know that we were together, but if I were to say now that I was there twice in August and twice in September, I really can't do that. I can't confirm that. And I can't really answer your question. I might have been twice in August. I might have been there three times. I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, according to the note of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the question may have been misunderstood, at least there is some risk. You said you do not know how many in August, how many in September. You were talking about three or four. Were all those three or for within these two months, or would they be in October or December as well? Or -- your hesitation, was that about to put them in August or September, or even outside that time-frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps there was some other events in October, November, or December. But I think that, as for these events that we're talking about, that these events, those four meetings took place in September and August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the note of the interview -- or the meeting you had with the Cermak Defence on the 2nd of September of this year, according to that note, it says that you told the Cermak Defence on the 2nd of September that the investigator who took your 2002 interview tried to portray General Gotovina as a negative person through his questions. Can you give me a specific example of a question that the investigator asked you back in 2002 that you think tried to portray General Gotovina as a negative person?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that, and I stand by that. In questions that were related to General Gotovina, he did, indeed, try to reduce this to some negative personality. And when I said that General Gotovina, for a time, was in Knin and then he led the operation, whether it was called the south -- that he was ready and capable with the Croatian Army of reaching Banja Luka, and, if need be, perhaps he would go on further. He laughed ironically at that, and from that I concluded that he was trying to provoke me as a Serb and a former commissioner to say something negative about General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So your conclusion that the investigator tried to portray General Gotovina as a negative person is based on the fact that he laughed ironically when you said that General Gotovina was ready and capable of reaching Banja Luka. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you give me any other specific example of a question that the investigator asked that you think tried to portray General Gotovina as a negative person?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing comes to mind just now, but there were probably more such instances.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we move, please, to page 4 of this document, and page 7 in the B/C/S. Page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'd like to direct your attention to the second paragraph on this page. Do you see that -- that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- I didn't understand why these things referred to Mostar, Dubrovnik, and other places. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's the paragraph. Now, you've made a specific correction to that paragraph on Tuesday, in fact. And I'd just like to ask you if you remember now what the correction is that you made to that paragraph there. If you could read that paragraph and tell me if you remember what correction you made.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the correction was not made on Tuesday but before that. And what it boils down to is this: I did not say looted property but property that had been taken, were being taken to Mostar and Dubrovnik. Because later on, talking to the director of the company from Cijan, dealing in disinfection and disinsection [as interpreted] for food, et cetera, I was -- I received information. And before that I had sent a letter to Mr. Prtenjaca who was in the head of the district, saying that the corn was going bad in the silos belonging to the "Agroprevreda" company and that a speedy intervention was needed to prevent the corn from going bad. The head of the county called up the company in charge of disinfection and disinsection, rat control, and as they found that the company was not able to deal with the situation itself, the corn was transported in trucks. Now, whether by chance or not, the trucks had Mostar number plates and Dubrovnik number plates. Now why? Because in Metkovic there's a company which dealt with the grinding of corn, and I think that in that way they managed to prevent the corn from going bad and the corn was all right for human consumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page seven of the English and page 12 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'd like to direct your attention to the first and third paragraphs on this page, because, according to the changes that you made on Tuesday, both of these paragraphs are completely incorrect. On Tuesday, you said that you never said anything even approaching what's in those paragraphs, that they're totally wrong. But, if you look at the middle paragraph, the second paragraph on the page, in September, when you made changes to your statement, you made a specific correction or clarification to that middle paragraph. You said, according to the 2nd of September statement that the sentence: "I was aware that soldiers from the Croatian Army were committing crimes in the rural areas needs to be explained further. Pasic said it would be wrong to give the impression that only soldiers committed crimes in the rural areas since it was also civilians and civilians in uniform, demobilized people. Pasic informed the Defence that he thinks he did not pay sufficient attention when he read his statement." Now, my question is: Can you explain how it is that in September you noticed there was a mistake to this particular paragraph, the second paragraph on the page, and you made a specific clarification to it; but you didn't notice either the paragraph before that one or the paragraph after that one, which you said, on Tuesday, were completely incorrect. Can you explain how you missed both of those two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm staying with the fact that I said -- and while I was commissioner of the Government of the Republic of Croatia in Knin that --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'm not asking you about the contents. I'm asking you how it is that in September you noticed that there was a problem with the second paragraph and you corrected it; but you didn't notice that either of the two paragraphs, either the one right before, or the one right after, were completely incorrect, because you only noticed that on Tuesday. Can you explain how that is, how you missed both those paragraphs in September.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain it. I don't have that on my screen, and I'm not allowed to use that here, so I can't really compare the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It should be on your screen.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in English and without any corrections on the other bit. I don't have the amended version, the corrected version.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. But, Mr. Pasic, I read to you the correction you made to the second paragraph. And I'm telling you that on Tuesday you said that the first paragraph and the third paragraph were completely wrong. You can take my word for that because it's in your evidence. And I'm asking you how it is that you noticed in September that theres with a problem with the second paragraph and you wanted to change that, but you didn't notice that the paragraph right before or the paragraph right after were completely wrong. Can you explain how you missed that in September.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't be angry, but I don't really understand what you're actually asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson is drawing your attention to the following: In September, you made a detailed correction on one paragraph in the statement you had given to the Office of the Prosecution. You didn't say anything about the paragraph before that; you didn't say or correct anything in the paragraph after that. Now, what Ms. Gustafson is interested to know is this week, Tuesday, you said, These two paragraphs - on which you did not make any comment in September - are totally wrong. And she doesn't understand why you didn't say that in September and why it is only now, on Tuesday, that you suddenly, or you come to the conclusion that these two paragraphs, being totally wrong, without having said a word about it in September. That's what she's asking you.
