utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably I analysed it more carefully. But regardless of that, you can be angry with me or not, I have to say that I still don't understand, unless I see the supplement in front of me, before me, unless I have the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that they were wrong. But, Ms. Gustafson, please read again what the witness said last Tuesday in respect of these. And, Mr. Pasic, we're not angry. We're just trying to find out what evidence, what exactly the content of the evidence is you're providing to this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, may I be allowed to take a look at the statement myself to see and then it will be easier for me to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may consult the statement you've given this Tuesday. The statement you've given to the OTP is on the screen, so you can see that on the screen; and Ms. Gustafson also will read what you said on Tuesday. But you may use your hard copy for that purpose as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, with respect to the first paragraph -- I'm sorry I don't know the page number of the correction in the B/C/S version, but it's at page 3 of the English version from your Tuesday statement. Where it states: "The police did not do anything. Perhaps some of them were involved. I think that some of the police who had been expelled from Knin earlier returned and were frustrated. If the military and police could protect churches and other buildings, why couldn't they protect the people?" On Tuesday you said that is completely incorrect. In respect of the second sentence, you said: "There were some policemen in Knin and in the area around Knin who were displaced in 1991. From 1991 until 1995, they worked as policemen in other areas of Croatia. In 1995, they returned to Knin." That was the correction you made to the first paragraph. And the correction you made to the third paragraph was, where it states: "Their units commanders could have stopped them. The commander of the Military District was Gotovina. He was away fighting elsewhere, but the command chain obviously wasn't functioning. Otherwise, the soldiers who were looting and destroying property would have been stopped. Even the government could have stopped them if it wanted to." And then it says: "Mr. Pasic said that he had not said that because he could not have known that." So, on Tuesday, you said that both the first paragraph on that -- on the screen and the third paragraph on the screen were completely incorrect, but back in September you made a specific clarification to the middle paragraph, and I read that out to you earlier. And my question is: If it's true that the first paragraph on the page and the third paragraph on the page are completely incorrect, why didn't you notice that in September, when you made a correction to the paragraph right in between those two paragraphs? Do you know -- do you have an explanation as to why you missed those two paragraphs in September?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I hadn't read the statement carefully enough, and I repeat that now. Tomorrow, or in a few days' time, if I were to look at them again, I might correct something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move to page nine of the English and page 14 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pasic, I would like to direct your attention to the middle of the page. And it's the paragraph that begins: "The military could have stopped the attacks in the villages." Sorry, that's my mistake. Sorry. Strike that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, on Tuesday, you have basically said that there are five paragraphs in your statement all dealing with the subject of either the police or the military failing to prevent or stop crimes that you say are now completely incorrect, and I'm going to read them to you. And the first one is point 2 of your statement from Tuesday where it states: "The cooperation with the police was not good because they didn't do what they could have done. What I mean by that is it the police did nothing at the beginning to protect the people and their property and encourage them to stay. They did nothing stop the civilians and military from looting. My relationship personally with Milos Mihic was good. I think that the mistake that the police made was that they used policemen from the area around Knin instead of using more policemen from other areas of Croatia. After Romanic left, the police coordinators didn't do anything. I don't know if they wouldn't or couldn't do anything. Nobody stopped the looting or burning down of houses." On Tuesday you said that that entire paragraph was incorrect, except for the sentence that said that your relationship with Milos Mihic had been good. Next one is point 3, where it says: "The police coordinators who were sent down from the ministry were in control of the police. That's why they were sent down. Either they couldn't or wouldn't do anything about the looting, or perhaps they had been told to keep their eyes closed." On Tuesday you said that was completely incorrect, that you had known that the minister of the interior had sent coordinators to help the police in the work -- in its work but had not known what their concrete tasks had been. The next one is point 7. And that's the one I read to you earlier about: "The police did not do anything. Perhaps some of them were involved. I think that some of the police who had been expelled from Knin earlier returned and were frustrated. If the military and police could protect churches and other buildings, why couldn't they protect the people?" You said that that was completely incorrect on Tuesday. And you said that there were some policemen in Knin who were displaced in 1991 who had returned to Knin in 1995. The next similar correction is point 8 from your statement on Tuesday, which says that -- where it states: "Their unit commanders could have stopped them. The commander of the Military District was Gotovina. He was away fighting elsewhere, but the command chain obviously wasn't functioning..." et cetera. And the last one is point 12, where it says: "The military could have stopped the attacks in the villages. There was no reason for them to go to the villages. There were only old people there. The only reason they went there would be to frighten and loot. They should have had a curfew to keep them in the barracks." And on Tuesday, you said that you had not said that because you simply did not know that. Now, each of these five paragraphs was read to you in 2002. You read them again in November of 2007. You read them again in February 2009. And you read them again, as you said, more carefully, just a few weeks ago, in September. And by my count, that's 20 times. And I get that by multiplying five different paragraphs of your statement by four different occasions when you reviewed your statement, that you have either read or had read to you a paragraph from your statement on this same subject, about the military or police failing to stop the crimes. Now, I understand you said you didn't read your statement as carefully as you should have, but even on a superficial reading of your statement, don't you think would you have noticed at least one of these five paragraphs on at least one of these four prior occasions that you now claim are totally incorrect? In other words, can you explain how you missed each and every one of those paragraphs on each and every one of those prior occasions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't read some things properly. I wasn't careful enough in reading them, and it is normal that some circumstances can change. Now, you quoted these paragraphs here, and I'm going to repeat some things for you. Without a doubt, on the territory of where Operation Storm went ahead, there were crimes committed. Nobody is challenging that. What is being challenged and what is contentious -- well, not even -- it is not even contentious who perpetrated the crimes. Crimes did occur. Now, as a commissioner, a responsible commissioner, on several occasions I contacted people and I set up meetings that the territory that was under me as a commissioner -- that crimes were being committed and that those crimes were being committed by persons in uniform. It is difficult now to say whether that particular person was a member of the Croatian Army, for instance. It could have been a member of the police or it could have been a civilian for that matter, because, during Operation Storm, hundreds and hundreds of thousands of people were mobilized. People were mobilized who had been demobilized previously. So any one of them could have committed that crime, and we pointed that out. Now, it was difficult to control an area with -- which covered a surface area of 1.049 square kilometres with the few people that we had. If I might be allowed to continue, I am not accusing the army of the -- or the police, somebody else should have prevented the crimes. And it was the military police who was in charge of that and the civilian police, the military prosecutor's office and the civilian prosecutor's office. And whether they are military prosecutors or the other prosecutors, whoever, and you must know that quite a lot of crimes were taken to court, were prosecuted, the perpetrators of those crimes were punished. Now, unfortunately, most of them will never see the light of justice and so, in my opinion, that is why these three men are being tried here and now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, on the subject of these three men who are being tried here now, virtually all the changes that you have made to your statement, either in September -- the recent ones in September, and then on Tuesday, virtually all of them result in a position that is more favourable to these accused. For example, negative comments about General Gotovina have turned into positive ones; repeated references to the military or the police being able to stop the crimes have been retracted; the comment that Serb returnees and those who stayed did not trust the police has been retracted; the comment that you believed the looting and burning was planned from above, you've retracted; comments that the military police was involved in the looting, you've retracted; comments that a lot of profit was made by the looting; the killings in the villages should not have happened, you've retracted. Mr. Pasic with all of these changes that you have made in September and again on Tuesday, the result is a fundamentally different statement and one that is markedly more favourable to these accused. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are entitled to your opinion, and I have given you mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the question is whether you agree with Ms. Gustafson that the overall picture in this statement, as you have given it now - and I'm talking about the picture since Tuesday - is more favourable to the accused than the overall picture which emerged from your previous statements. The question is whether you agree with that or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the question comes up, whether you consider that it's still the same; or that the new statement is less favourable, the picture from the new statement is less favourable for the accused; or didn't it change anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry if the new statement is more -- more unfavourable to them. To me, these are facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't say that the new one is more unfavourable. You were asked about whether you consider your new statement to be equally favourable or unfavourable to the accused, or whether you consider the new statement to be more favourable to the accused, or whether you consider your new statement less favourable for the accused. Now three options: More favourable, the same, less favourable. That's what Ms. Gustafson, at least, started to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't consider it in the light of being more favourable or less favourable. I said that it was the truth, and I said that if it's less favourable, I'm sorry. And if it's -- well, the fact of the matter is that what I have now stated is the truth. I cannot gauge what is or what is not favourable to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When you said that if your statement was less favourable to the accused you're sorry, do you want your statement to be favourable to the accused?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't giving my statement in order to make it favourable or not favourable to the accused. I gave my view of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, I'm going to suggest to you that the real reason that you have made all of these changes to your statement in September and in October is not because you didn't say these things. I'm going to suggest to you that you did say these things in 2002 and you did believe them to be true at the time and that the real reason you've made all of these changes in the last few weeks is because you don't want your evidence to implicate the accused. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are here to put your case, whatever it may be. I came here to tell the truth, since I was an eye-witness of all these events. You, Madam Prosecutor, have a piece of paper, and I have a clear picture of my -- in my mind of everything that happened and that I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move now to another topic. You've given evidence that you attended meetings that were held every day in General Cermak's office. And my question for you is: Now, who told that you there were to be meetings every day in General Cermak's office that you were to attend? How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Knin as a commissioner of the government of the Republic of Croatia, the conditions I found in the office in Knin at the time were at the minimum. The only service or structure that could provide any assistance was the army. Not even the police was able to help us, since their premises had been devastated just before the departure of the forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just going to interrupt you. Your statements are in evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one matter. I don't see anywhere reference that he was told to go to meetings and perhaps the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But -- well, How did you learn that? --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's try to focus the witness's attention on the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You met on a daily basis, Mr. Pasic, in what I understand to be Mr. -- General Cermak's office. How did you find out that there would be a meeting where you were expected to attend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the first meeting that we had, it was agreed that we would be in contact when necessary. Perhaps where it was said once or twice daily is not really reflective of the truth. We may have met, as the situation dictated, more than once, maybe five to seven times on certain days. Now, how did this come about? Well, at the first meeting where we agreed on what sort of coordination activity we would have, it was said a meeting would take place on the following day at 9.00 or at such and such an hour, and whoever was able to, attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, how did you know to go to this first meeting that you're talking about? How did you find out about the first meeting where it was agreed on what sort of coordination activity we would have?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was natural that, upon my arrival in Knin, I had to find an interlocutor with whom I would be able to solve the problems. I met that individual in the person of Mr. Cermak, and he was the one I contacted. If I may only add this, several meetings, which isn't something that was stated here, were held in the office of the commissioner of the Republic of Croatia as soon as circumstances permitted it, because it simply provided better conditions, in terms of conditioning, air-conditioning, coffee, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said: "Upon my arrival in Knin, I had to find an interlocutor with him I would be able to solve the problems. I met that individual in the person of Mr. Cermak."

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you to go to Mr. Cermak, or did you just walk around Knin until you happened upon him? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall first have to explain to you that the Commission of the Republic of Croatia, which acted in exile, had very few staff. It made a big difference if one worked as a commissioner for the Republic of Croatia for the displaced persons. Well, I didn't go in search of him about the town. I found out that he was appointed garrison commander, and I went to see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Who -- who told you that he was appointed garrison commander? How did you find out that General Cermak was appointed garrison commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I heard the news on the Croatian television. Let me tell you, as a matter of fact, it was the County Prefect of the Zadar-Knin county, Mr. Sime Prtenjaca, who informed me about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did Mr. Prtenjaca tell you to go and speak with Mr. Cermak when you arrived in Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement to the Prosecution, you said that General Cermak directed you to organise the feeding of people and pushed you to open the stores. Can you be a little more specific about this? What exactly did General Cermak say to you when he directed you to organise the feeding of people and push you to open the stores?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following the military and police Operation Storm, the majority of the population that stayed behind and that had returned upon the call of the Croatian government were unable to either stay in their homes or cook meals there. On his office premises, General Cermak organised a soup kitchen, that's how we call it, for those who didn't have the wherewithal to cook their means -- meals, and I was involved in that exercise. As soon as the numbers of people who availed themselves of the soup kitchen increased beyond every measure, Mr. Cermak advised me to help the people by opening up a soup kitchen in the premises of what was formally a restaurant, and, in fact, some 300 to 400 meals were served a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, it didn't involve only the population of Croatia, and let me tell you, Mr. Cermak and I did not distinguish between the various backgrounds, whether it was a Croat, or Muslim, or a Serb, when it came to helping then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like you to focus as much as you can on the specific question that I'm asking: You said: "Mr. Cermak advised me to help the people by opening up a soup kitchen." Do you remember now what exactly General Cermak said to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim that with 100 percent certainty, but he said that the premises of the Croatian Army, the hall -- the mess hall of the Croatian Army was no longer the suitable place for a soup kitchen, and that appropriate quarters needed to be found where the soup kitchen could relocate to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And General Cermak either directed or advised you to do certain things. Did you do them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on what his advice had to do with.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you think of any instance when he directed or advised you to do something and you didn't do it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Cermak -- well, I was not duty-bound to implement some of his decisions. I only cooperated with him. I did not consider him to be my superior, although I, as a person, do believe that a rank of a colonel or general is a high position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question was whether you remember anything you were advised or directed to do which you didn't do. You were not asked to elaborate on what your duties were, but just to give an example of something you were advised or directed to do which you then decided not to do. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be a good idea to have a look at the tasks that I was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Give -- give us an example. That's what Ms. Gustafson is asking you to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cermak did not give me any assignments or tasks. I had my work remit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Earlier you were asked if General Cermak either directed or advised you to do certain things, whether you would do them. Your answer was: "It depended on what his advice had to do with." Now, we are waiting for an example of something General Cermak directed or advised you to do, where you decided not to do it. Just an example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't really find an example that would tie in with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's an answer to the question. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please have D504 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I don't know whether -- I'm looking at the clock. I don't know whether you're enter a new area.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. And I think it should be quite brief on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If could you look at the document on your screen, please, Mr. Pasic. You can see this is an order dated 11 October 1995, and it's to the MUP Knin police station and the Commission of the Government of the Republic of Croatia for Knin municipality. And it says: "On the basis of demonstrated needs and in order to be more operative, I hereby order: ... a part of the MUP officers with the Knin police station shall be temporarily transferred to the old grammar school building in Knin ..." And it says: "This order shall enter into force immediately." And it's signed by General Cermak. Did you -- do you recall receiving this order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that it was addressed, but I can't remember. It probably did reach us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you remember receiving any other similar orders from General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, this order is not directed to me or my office. I had never received an order from General Cermak. This order is addressed to the MUP Knin police station and was sent to my attention only, for -- for my information.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you remember at all whether this order was implemented, whether MUP officers were, in fact, temporarily transferred to the old grammar school building in Knin about this time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm seeing that members of the MUP were quartered in the secondary school building. They did have a police station in Knin, but I guess the school building had to be placed at the disposal of the broadcasting services or whoever. But to my knowledge, General Cermak was not superior to the police force in order to be able to issue orders to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I wasn't asking you about that. I was asking you whether the MUP officers were, in fact, transferred to the old grammar school building. Do you remember whether that transfer actually took place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions on this document, so perhaps it's a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break and I'd like to reserve some -- close to ten minutes after the break to start with some procedural matters, which would mean that the further cross-examination would start at approximately 1.00. Ms. Gustafson, could you give us any indication as to how much more time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I will try to finish before the end of the day, but I can't guarantee it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, may I take it that you would need considerable time in re-cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know about considerable. That depends on -- I was intending to address the issue with the Chamber as to my 90(H) obligations in this particular circumstance, which I think is somewhat unique. Depending on what the Chamber believes my 90(H) obligation to be, and it could be extensive. Without dealing with the 90(H), I do have some matters that I would like to clarify in cross-examination which might take up to a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, it's unlikely that we would finish today. Mr. Kay, would there be any need to re-exam the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this moment, I only have one question to re-examine on. At the moment, nothing else arises for me. And it obviously depends on any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. And the Markac Defence, same position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Same position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd first like to revisit the 92 bis issue I briefly referred to yesterday, because the Chamber would now like to extend an invitation to the parties with regard to the six 92 bis motions, which were filed by the Cermak Defence on the 2nd of October. The motions concern 17 witnesses and the material that the Cermak Defence seeks to have admitted into evidence, including transcripts, witness statements, an associated exhibits. That material amounts to around 1500 pages. The Chamber has not studied the material in detail yet, but the submissions by the Cermak Defence indicate that the material covers crimes committed by Serb forces in the Krajina before the Indictment period in this case. The Cermak Defence argues that the material supports its thesis that individuals were motivated by revenge during Operation Storm. The Chamber notes in this respect that the six Rule 92 bis motions are all very similar and therefore give no, or limited, guidance as to what the Cermak Defence would like to draw to the Chamber's attention to with regard to each piece of tendered evidence. Yesterday, the Chamber informed the parties that it wished to discuss the motions and the best way for the Cermak Defence to present the material contained therein. Already in its decision on the Cermak Defence's request to disclose Rule 68 material of the 7th of August, 2009, the Chamber encouraged the parties to engage in a process which would lead to a submission of agreed facts on the matter. This was based on the arguments made by the Prosecution at that time, that it did not dispute the facts that the Cermak Defence sought to prove through the relevant material. As the Chamber has indicated on previous occasions, it is for the parties to review evidentiary material to identify what is relevant and what they find important for this case and then tender only that material. It is not acceptable to tender huge amounts of material with the expectation that the Chamber will do this task for the parties. Considering the nature and the scope of the matters that the Cermak Defence apparently wishes to demonstrate with the extensive material it has tendered, the Chamber considers that the Cermak Defence should seek other avenues for its admission. The details surrounding each incident described by the 17 witnesses appear not to be of importance to the present case. Moreover, as previous submissions in this case indicate, it is not a matter of dispute that crimes were committed by Serb forces in the Krajina prior to the Indictment period. And under these circumstances, the Chamber still considers that the most appropriate way for the Cermak Defence to present the relevant and important portions of the material is through agreed facts. Since the material, to a large extent stems from the Martic case, the Cermak Defence might also consider introducing it through adjudicated facts, in case agreement cannot be reached. The Chamber hereby reiterates its invitation of 7 August 2009 instructing the parties to make renewed efforts to reach agreement on a short statement of facts which could replace the lengthy submissions by the Cermak Defence. The parties should report back to the Chamber on their progress no later than the 27th of October, 2009. In the meantime, the Prosecution and the other Defence teams are not expected to respond to the six Rule 92 bis motions. And this concludes the Chamber's invitation. I would like to continue with, given the Chamber' guidance, on a practical aspect of receiving bar table submissions. On 28 September 2009, the Chamber emphasised the importance of having a transparent record of all matters brought to the attention of the Chamber that are not just of a mere practical nature. This can be found at transcript pages 22.183 to 22.185. In the past, and in relation to bar table submissions, the Chamber's practice has been to informally receive a spreadsheet from the parties, which, amongst other things, contained possible objections with regard to the admissibility of certain documents. In previous situations, the Chamber addressed any such objections or comments in court or in filed decisions, so as to put the informally voiced objections or comments on the record. One such example can be found at transcript pages 14.110 to 14.112. The Chamber notes, however, that certain objections to or comments on bar table submissions, although always dually considered, may not have been put on the record previously. The Chamber therefore invites the parties to review the record and, no later than the 6th of November, 2009, jointly file a list of all bar table submissions that involved informally communicated spreadsheets. In this list, the parties are invited to note for which bar table submissions and informally communicated objections or comments were clearly put on the record and include references. For bar table submissions not falling in this category, the parties are invited to attach the respective spreadsheets to their joint filing. For the future, the Chamber invites the parties to submit their joint spreadsheets for bar table submissions in a joint filing. I add to that, that in line with this invitation, the latest spreadsheet concerning the bar table submission on housing laws, e-mailed to the Chamber staff by the Gotovina Defence on 29th of September, 2009, should also be filed. And this concludes the Chamber's guidance. I move to another subject. That is, the suspect interview given by Mr. Cermak. We have received - and I'm referring to the suspect interview in which Mr. Karolj Dondo was present - we have received a transcript of exchanges between Mr. Cermak and Mr. Dondo in English recently. Could I first inquire with the Prosecution whether this transcript covers all the exchanges between Mr. Cermak and Mr. Dondo, or whether that is a selection?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd have to make inquiries on that, Your Honour. We can probably get back to you in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then hear from you. The Chamber would like - and we'll later hear whether it's a complete set or it is a selection, and if it is a selection, what is the basis for this selection. But the Chamber would like to have this suspect interview to be completed in such a way that, attached to the English version of the transcript of the interview, that we'd find the exchanges between Mr. Dondo and Mr. Cermak, and that we -- references should be given in the text of the interview where such exchanges occurred. So that when reading the English text that our attention will be drawn to any exchanges which we'll then find transcribed in an attachment to that statement. And the chamber would like to know whether we have a complete set or not, in order to see whether we could give further guidance. Of course, if the set is complete, there's nothing more to be said. If the set is incomplete, we'll further consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we'll attend to that right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I finally would like to put the following on the record. As all parties are aware, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Rules 92 bis, 92 ter, 92 quater, deal with the use of written statements. Apart from what we find in the Rules, also some case law has been developed by this Tribunal - and I'm specifically referring to the Limaj and the Popovic case - case law related to the use of previous inconsistent statements. That case law includes procedural implications, such as whether or not one would have to declare a witness hostile. Now, the question could arise as to how the set of rules, as we find them in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, would relate to what we -- what was developed in the case law, whether, if we're talking about 92 ter statements, for example, whether a similar mechanism as to previous inconsistent statements but then not compared to testimony given at trial but, for example, other statements, whether, at all, you could rely upon parts of a 92 ter statement to which a witness distanced himself of, at a later stage, whether there would be any procedural implications, whether one could admit this at all, whether, as far as procedural implications, for example, if a cross-examining party would rely on a previous statement, that might be different. Well, the parties are hereby informed that this rather complex legal issue came to the mind of the Chamber - the Chamber has not formed any opinion about these matters - but if the parties, if the same legal issue would ever have come to the minds of the parties, and if the parties would want to share their views or to assist the Chamber in developing its thoughts by providing their views on the matter, whether now or at a later stage, the parties are certainly not discouraged from doing so. That is what I would like to put on the record. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I guess I will take the opportunity extended by the Chamber, if I may, with leave of the Chamber, to address the issue now. At least a portion of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would like to do it right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, just one portion which is so that I know how to again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- proceed with what might transpire next. As I read Rule 90(H) subpart (ii) there is a duty to put the nature of the case which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness. And I just want to state for the record that my understanding of that is that this witness, if he is being impeached with a prior statement, that that impeachment is not in contradiction of the evidence he is giving. If the Chamber is of a different view and would instead accept that as substantive testimony of the witness, I am prepared to proceed to challenge those portions of the 2002 statement. I also wish to add, however, that it would be our submission that a party relying on a prior inconsistent statement that is seeking to use the portions of that statement as substantive testimony, nevertheless, should then establish foundation for some of the matters that are raised. I note specifically that many of the things that were in the 2002 statement are conclusions in fact and not facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that the parties would easily agree that there are quite some portions in the 2002 statement which are rather opinion or conclusions than facts. We find a bit of everything in it. But I take it that you would not disagree with that, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, in this case I don't see any difference between this instance and many prior instances when conclusions appear in witness's 92 ter statement and the Chamber assigns the appropriate weight to those conclusions based on the foundation in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's precisely the point I wish to make, Mr. President, is that if the Prosecution were or had -- has the intention of relying on conclusions that don't have a foundation in the statement, then while we're still on cross-examination, I believe the Chamber -- the Prosecution or the party relying on a prior inconsistent conclusion would have a duty to try to establish some foundation for that conclusion while we're still here. Obviously, that would then impact the probative value of relying on a prior inconsistent statement at least with respect to conclusions in it, if in fact no foundation was established in the statement nor in the examination of the witness. And the reason I raise this is quite simply to -- for us as a Defence to engage in a re-cross of a witness who disavows the conclusions in the statement really amounts to a waste of time. And just simply going through an exercise of making a record that we put our -- the nature of our case to the witness under 90(H) but the witness consistently saying that I didn't say that or those are not my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there are really two issues here, and I think that the first one I disagree with and the second one I think I agree with. The first is the duty to establish a foundation. It's my understanding that the practice of this Chamber is that if there's a conclusion that a witness draws in a 92 ter statement, if a party wants to rely on that conclusion and doesn't elicit a sufficient foundation for it, then the Chamber will not assign that conclusion much weight. But I've not understood the practice in this trial as placing an obligation on a party to explore the foundation for every conclusion in a statement. The second issue is the 90(H) issue. And it's my understanding that the 90(H) rule is essentially a rule of fairness to the witness, that the witness should be confronted with the contrary state of -- contrary case of the cross-examining party. And to that extent, if the witness disavows something in a prior statement, I don't see why another cross-examining party would have an obligation to put their case that contradicts something that the witness has disavowed because the fairness issue doesn't arise. The Chamber, at the end of the day, can assign whatever weight they deem appropriate to the original statement and the later disavowal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me already make a few comments. First of all, I was talking about 92 ter. Of course, a similar question is that the matter I raised before could be raised in -- in relation to expert reports. And there, of course, the issue of conclusions becomes far more prominent than it would be with a witness of fact. Having added that, let me just confirm with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The court participants are kindly asked to switch off the microphones that are not in use, because at some points it is almost impossible to hear Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In a short consultation, I briefly discussed with my colleagues that we are -- we have two rather distinct situations. The first situation is where a witness draws conclusions and does not provide a factual basis for such conclusions. Now, witnesses of fact, of course, are not supposed to present conclusions and opinions, but, rather -- nevertheless, we also know that sometimes people are inclined to put matters in terms of conclusions. And I think the Chamber has earlier said a few words about that. Without a proper factual basis, the Chamber is not in a position to verify or to adopt conclusions similar to the conclusions of the witness. So, therefore, and that's a general rule, and has got nothing to do, I take it, with whether the statements were inconsistent or not. But if it's just conclusions without a proper factual basis, the Chamber is simply not in a position to draw similar conclusions on the basis of the testimony of that witness. Perhaps there is other evidence which could lead the Chamber to adopt conclusions which are similar or different from the conclusions by that witness, but that's, I would say, a rather general situation. The second situation is a quite different one. That is, where the witness says, I haven't said A, B, or, C, or D, as it appears in my statement. That is exactly the area I referred to earlier where the Chamber is still considering this legal issue and, of course, it depends on the outcome of this, I would say, legal exercise, which we are only at the beginning of. I would say the first step being to define what exactly the issue is. Whether, at the end, we could rely on information provided by the witness in a statement, which he does not confirm at trial. But that's, of course, a situation to be distinguished from the other situation I just mentioned. Therefore, Mr. Misetic, if a witness gives a statement and says, General X, Y, or Z, has, in my opinion, not always met his obligations as a member of the local tennis club, without giving any further information, then, of course, there's no need to go into that in any further detail, because whether he did or did not, there's no factual basis for that, unless, in his statement, we would find how often he attended, whether he trained well, et cetera. So, therefore, if it's clear that conclusions and final conclusions are to be drawn by the Chamber have no factual basis, it doesn't make much sense to put to the witness that, in relation to this matter, the party cross-examining him would have another opinion, because that doesn't make sense. Now, on the other matter - and we were talking about Rule 90(H) to the fairness of the witness - that if a party considers there's inconsistency and may even have doubts as to which of the two, whether that's a statement or testimony, would be of a kind to be believed rather than the other one, more reliable, more credible than the other one, then, of course, it should be clearly put to that witness that there is an inconsistency and that he is invited to explain such an inconsistency, something where we're talking about inconsistency between testimony and statements. That is it usually, I would say, almost automatically done anyhow, because that's in the interests of the party cross-examining that witness. Does this give you sufficient guidance, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but there are just two points to raise. One is the 90(H) issue. We were prepared to attempt to discredit the matters in the 2002 statement based purely on the substance of it. So we're at somewhat of a disadvantage in terms of counsel for the Prosecution posits it as, if a party doesn't challenge the foundation of a statement, then there's probative value regardless of whether it's an opinion or a factual statement; the Chamber is free to evaluate the probative value of that. However, that doesn't take into account the fact that there may be information in our possession which would actually further discredit the opinions in the 2002 statement. So that's position we finds ourselves in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that -- if that's your first point, let me just -- or would you like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will just complete the second point as well because I want to be transparent on what our intention is in re-cross. And it's related to the point Your Honour, that you're raising about 92 ter and assessing whether to rely on the statement that the witness has not adopted versus the statement that the witness is currently adopting. We intend to explore in re-cross the methodology and methods used by the OTP investigator in 2002 which resulted in some of the statements that appear -- some of the conclusions without foundation that are littered throughout the 2002 statement. To that end, the same investigator appeared in suspect interviews of other people which we have on video and are ready to use, where he says things like, Witness, the Prosecution says there was a plan and that plan was to expel people and to burn their houses and to loot and to prevent them coming back; do you agree? And the witness is then put in a position of either accepting the proposition or rejecting it. We think this witness, it should be explored, if in fact this has now become an issue, whether the conclusions concerning whether the top of the state approved criminal activity, et cetera, is in fact the result of similar leading of a witness, to use a phrase, putting words in his mouth, and then asking a witness, who's in a position of being interviewed by a Prosecutor's office at an international Tribunal, whether he agrees or disagrees with it. So we intend to explore further the reliability of the 2002 statement, and part of my cross-examination the Chamber will note is in fact the witness started in 1996 taking the position that he has taken today, and it's, in fact, this statement in 2002 that is somewhat different than what he said -- actually substantial different than what he said in 1996 and in 2009. But I wanted to the Chamber to hear that outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the Prosecution, at certain moments, primarily focussed on credibility, reliability. Is it your later statement that you didn't say any of these things at an earlier stage, true or not? Of course, no determination on what is most credible has been made and, as I outlined before, there is a legal issue involved here which is rather complex. Now, the Chamber thinks that it makes sense to -- where we could not yet for sure exclude for the possibility that the earlier -- the previous statement could serve as evidence. I'm not giving any ruling on that. But as we invited the parties, you may have understood that the Chamber is just considering that legal issue. If we consider a legal issue, then that means that there's no outcome yet. So, therefore, we could not exclude or you could not conclude at this moment as a possible outcome that the Chamber would consider that what was said at the time, as we find it in the statement, is what the witness really said, apart from whether that would be conclusions or -- and whatever to do with that and whatever weight to give to that, that's all open. If you can't exclude for that possibility, then, of course, it still makes sense to challenge in cross-examination the substance of what the witness would have had said and of which we do not know yet whether that could be adopted. The second issue is -- and that, of course, also takes into consideration that you could not exclude the possibility that words were spoken as reported. Of course, it then makes sense to further explore the techniques used during the interviews so as to see to what extent, if one were to conclude that the words spoken as reported or as put on paper, that in order to give any weight to that, or to further consider what the evidentiary value of that would be, to explore these interviewing techniques. So on both issue, the Chamber doesn't think that it would not make sense to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We agree, Mr. President, and we will conduct ourselves accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have 12 minutes left. It took a bit more time, but these are rather fundamental issues so therefore the Chamber considered it appropriate to raise those matters. And I must say, just for your information, that it's not on the basis of what happens today in court or what happened yesterday in court, but that the Chamber was already earlier considering to at least raise the issue as something the Chamber was thinking about, just in order to avoid any misunderstanding as to it being raised today. Mr. Misetic, I take it that you would have some -- for the first ten minutes -- no, but it's Mr. Kay, of course, who should have an opportunity to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution is still in cross-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. Yes. I even remember that you hoped, Ms. Gustafson, that you would finish your cross-examination in the next session. I think that we should give up that hope, isn't it? Yes. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you see when focussing on cross-examination by the Defence you might forget about your right to cross-examine the witness. Thank you, Mr. Pasic. Again, apologies for the delay. We'll not spend much time in court anymore today, and we would like to continue on Monday. But we have still some time left, and Ms. Gustafson will continue her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, right before the break, we were looking at an order issued by General Cermak, and you said: "To my knowledge, General Cermak was not superior to the police in order to be able to issue orders to them." You said that just before the break. And my question is: Did you know that General Cermak did, in fact, issue orders to the police, such as the one you had -- such as the one you had looked at right before the break. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to move to another topic, but I just had one follow-up question on something you said earlier today. And it was about the songs that you said had been sung at social events that you attended, that General Gotovina also attended. And one of the songs you identified was the song you called Jure and Boban; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence of a song which the first two lines of are: "Evo Zore, Evo Dana, Evo Jure i Bobana. Here comes the dawn, here comes the day, here come Jure and Boban." My question is: The song Jure and Boban that you referred to, is that this song, is it the same song that I --

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on to another topic, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, is there agreement between the parties what these songs are? I mean, are there various versions of the song? I mean, I don't know whether you want to ever present that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- there was a fair amount of evidence about this song and in particular the first two lines of that song. That came in through the witness Barkovic, and I think it's -- I think the connection is clear. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not a contested issue is what exactly the text of the song is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness's earphones be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pasic, could you take your earphones off, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President the words of the song are not contested. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... any type of singing is contested. And as I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think before re-cross --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's a different matter, whether the song was sung yes or no is another matter. But at least if we are talking about -- we have dealt now with the first two lines and it's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if I could just state that in re-cross the Chamber will be entertained with the entire two-hour concert if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think Ms. Gustafson dealt with three or four social events where songs apparently were sung so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which is also contested, and I will go into that in re-cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But we'll get audios of those other as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually we've located all the singers who happened to all be on the one video as opposed to four separate occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll hear later, literally. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, on this issue of putting matters, I don't know how significant the song is or the interpretation of the words or whether it's the position that the Prosecution are going to say that this song is interpreted a particular way, to my mind, that's a classic example where you should put your interpretation to the witness if you're going seek to get the Bench to draw a particular conclusion on this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness changed his qualification of the song, at least as it was put on paper from a Chetnik song to a patriotic song. Now, if the Chamber would ever be -- or would be called to see whether this is any significant change, it might be that we'd have to know the exact text of the song. And that's the only reason why I asked whether there was any dispute about that, and how reasonable one qualification or the other would be. Could you please put on your earphones again. And I had forgotten about the other piece of evidence, then, apparently. Ms. Gustafson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, in your Defence statement, you identified the commander of the military police in Knin as Luka Orsulic. And my question is: Do you remember a person named Bosko Dzolic, who was the commander of the military police in Knin up until the 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said also in your Defence statement that you didn't see the military police in attendance at the meetings that General Cermak held in his office. Is that right? Do I understand your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received a substantial amount of evidence regarding the people who attended these meetings with General Cermak. And other participants at those meetings have given evidence that the military police were, in fact, present at those meetings. And these include Mr. Dzolic, who was, before Mr. Orsulic, the military police commander in Knin, who testified that he attended three regular briefings that General Cermak held at about 10.00 in the morning in his office building; Mr. Dondo also testified that representatives of the military police attended meetings that General Cermak held in the morning; and General Cermak has given statements to the Prosecution in which he sated that he had meetings in his office with the military police and the civilian police. Do you think you might be mistaken about whether the military police were present at morning meetings in General Cermak's office?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot state that they were or were not in attendance. But what I can confirm, and I do once more, that members of the military police were not present at the meetings that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm about to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we should adjourn. Before which do so, Ms. Gustafson, the completeness of the exchanges between Mr. Cermak and Mr. Dondo, could you inform the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, I am informed that it is P2526, which is the exhibit that contains those exchanges, is in fact complete. It includes everything, every exchange that was in the interview. And we can arrange with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P2526. These are the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's the interview itself, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm misreading my note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But it is everything that been translated from that interview on to the additional document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the English transcript of the exchanges between Mr. Cermak and Mr. Dondo completely reflect whatever was said between them as transcribed in B/C/S and -- as audible? Then we do not need any further discussion. Then you are -- the Prosecution is invited to insert in P2526 references to the exchanges transcribed in this new document, so that we would clearly see where the exchange is to be located in time; then to attach those transcripts to P2526; and then to upload this new version to be admitted into evidence as a replacement of P2526 as it is now uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we adjourn. Mr. Pasic, I give you the same instructions as I did yesterday. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That you should not speak - and there's a whole weekend not to speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given yesterday or today or still to be given next week - not to speak with anyone about your testimony, and we'd like to see you back, Monday, 9.00 in the morning, in Courtroom I, because we'll adjourn and we will resume at -- on Monday, the 12th of October, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 12th day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
